content: The VUKA family program was piloted as a family-based psychosocial intervention aimed at improving health and mental health outcomes among early adolescents living with HIV in South Africa. This study was published in AIDS Care in 2014. Project nGage evaluated the effectiveness of a dyadic network support intervention to retain young Black men who have sex with men in HIV care. The results of this randomized controlled trial were published in AIDS Behavior in 2017. A study by Belzer et al. investigated the use of cell phone support to improve medication adherence among HIV-infected youth and young adults who were non-adherent. This initial randomized controlled trial was published in AIDS Behavior in 2014. Willis et al. assessed the effectiveness of Community Adolescent Treatment Supporters (CATS) interventions in improving linkage to care, retention in care, adherence to antiretroviral therapy (ART), and psychosocial well-being among adolescents living with HIV in rural Zimbabwe. The findings were published in BMC Public Health in 2019. Mavhu et al. conducted a cluster-randomized controlled trial in Zimbabwe to evaluate the impact of a differentiated service delivery model (Zvandiri) on virological failure among adolescents living with HIV. The results were published in The Lancet Global Health in 2020. Whiteley et al. explored the use of an iPhone game to enhance health outcomes among youth living with HIV. This study was published in AIDS Care in 2018. Garofalo et al. conducted a randomized controlled trial to assess the impact of personalized text message reminders on medication adherence among HIV-positive adolescents and young adults. The findings were published in AIDS Behavior in 2016. Linnemayr et al. evaluated the use of text messaging to improve adherence to antiretroviral therapy among adolescents and young adults. The study found no significant effects after one year and was published in American Journal of Public Health in 2017. Dulli et al. tested the effectiveness of a social media-based support group intervention (SMART Connections) for youth living with HIV in Nigeria. This randomized controlled trial was published in Journal of Medical Internet Research in 2020. Spratt et al. reviewed research and methods for using technology to improve adherence to HIV medications among transitional-age youth. Lessons learned were published in Journal of General Medicine in 2017. Bermudez et al. investigated whether economic strengthening interventions could improve viral suppression among adolescents living with HIV in Uganda. The results of this cluster-randomized trial were published in AIDS Behavior in 2018. Christodoulou et al. explored the use of active visualizations to understand medication adherence among youth living with HIV. This study was published in AIDS Behavior in 2019. Nestadt et al. piloted a family-based psychosocial intervention (CHAMP+ Thailand) for perinatally HIV-infected early adolescents. The findings were published in AIDS Patient Care and STDs in 2019. Kaihin et al. evaluated the impact of an empowerment intervention on antiretroviral drug adherence among Thai youth. The study was published in Behavioral Medicine in 2015. Berrien et al. demonstrated that adherence to antiretroviral therapy in HIV-infected pediatric patients improved with a home-based intensive nursing intervention. This study was published in AIDS Patient Care and STDs in 2004. Brown et al. conducted a controlled trial to assess the treatment of depressive disorders in medical clinics for adolescents and young adults living with HIV. The findings were published in Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2016. Denison et al. evaluated the impact of a clinic-based peer mentoring program (Project YES.) on viral suppression, adherence, and internalized stigma among HIV-positive youth in Zambia. The results were published in PLOS One in 2020. Han et al. conducted a systematic review on eHealth literacy among people living with HIV. The findings were published in JMIR Public Health and Surveillance in 2018. Fatti et al. assessed the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of community-based support for adolescents receiving antiretroviral treatment in South Africa. This operational research study was published in Journal of the International AIDS Society in 2018. Bermudez et al. conducted a cluster-randomized trial in Uganda to evaluate the impact of economic strengthening on viral suppression among adolescents living with HIV. The findings were published in AIDS Behavior in 2018. Brothers et al. examined outcomes from a targeted secondary prevention empowerment pilot trial for young women living with HIV. The study was published in AIDS Patient Care and STDs in 2016. Mark et al. analyzed data from 324 facilities in 30 countries to optimize HIV service delivery for infants, children, and adolescents. The findings were presented in a report accessible online. Vojnov et al. conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on the performance of non-laboratory staff in diagnostic testing and specimen collection in HIV programs. The study was published in PLOS One in 2019. Luo et al. reviewed the clinical impact of point-of-care early infant diagnosis for HIV. The findings are in preparation for publication. Drain et al. validated the use of a clinic-based cryptococcal antigen lateral flow assay for screening HIV-infected adults in South Africa. The study was published in Scientific Reports in 2019. Wake et al. evaluated the performance of point-of-care cryptococcal antigen screening using finger-prick blood. The findings were published in Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2018. Williams et al. assessed the diagnostic accuracy of a fingerstick cryptococcal antigen lateral flow assay in HIV-infected individuals. The study was published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2015. Olugbenga et al. conducted a clinic-based evaluation of the diagnostic accuracy of a dual rapid test for HIV and syphilis screening in pregnant women in Nigeria. The findings were published in PLOS One in 2018. Gous et al. explored the feasibility of performing multiple point-of-care tests for HIV antiretroviral treatment initiation and monitoring using single or multiple fingersticks. The study was published in PLOS One in 2013. Gous et al. implemented multiple point-of-care testing in two HIV antiretroviral treatment clinics in South Africa. The findings were published in Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2016. Jani et al. demonstrated the accuracy of CD4 T-cell enumeration and antiretroviral drug toxicity monitoring using point-of-care testing in primary healthcare clinics. The study was published in AIDS in 2011. Drain et al. combined point-of-care HIV viral load testing with task shifting to improve treatment outcomes in an open-label, non-inferiority randomized controlled trial. The findings were published in The Lancet HIV in 2020. Le Roux et al. conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis comparing the clinical and operational impact of point-of-care versus laboratory-based nucleic acid testing for routine HIV viral load monitoring. The findings are in preparation for publication. The World Health Organization published updated recommendations on service delivery for the treatment and care of people living with HIV, emphasizing the integration of multidisease testing devices in laboratory networks. This report was published in 2020. Unitaid released a report on the multidisease diagnostic landscape for integrated management of HIV, HCV, TB, and other coinfections. The report was published in 2018. Obure et al. conducted a comparative analysis of the costs of single and dual rapid HIV and syphilis diagnostics in Colombia. The findings were published in Sexually Transmitted Infections in 2017. Khan and Vojnov reviewed the patient impact and programmatic advantages of integrated testing. The findings are in preparation for publication. Ndlovu et al. conducted a feasibility study on multidisease testing for HIV and TB using the GeneXpert platform in rural Zimbabwe. The findings were published in PLOS One in 2018. The Clinton Health Access Initiative evaluated the patient impact, programmatic advantages, and cost savings of integrated testing. The findings are in preparation for publication.
